title: Thermal Pleasure and Alliesthesia in the Built Environment
research_question: To propose the physiological concept of alliesthesia as a suitable framework for understanding thermal environmental perception under dynamic or non-isothermal conditions, and to provide empirical evidence for its operation in different thermoregulatory zones and under localized thermal stimuli (contact heating and air movement).

participants.description: Paper 2: 13 university-aged subjects (6 women, 7 men). Paper 3: 53 university-aged subjects (20 women, 33 men), reduced to n=29 for feet warming and n=46 for hand warming after exclusions. Paper 4: 35 university-aged subjects (9 women, 26 men) after exclusions.
participants.recruitment: University-aged subjects, advised to refrain from strenuous exercise, alcohol, tobacco, or caffeine 12 hours prior to experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Paper 2: Series of temperature step-changes (e.g., 24.5°C to 28°C, 24.5°C to 20°C) and ramps, interspersed with periods of increased metabolic activity (cycling) and local thermal control options (fan, heat lamps).
Paper 3: Localized warming to hands and feet (Peltier cells on aluminum panels) in a cool ambient environment (21.5°C).
Paper 4: Four air movement patterns (constant, sinusoidal, square-wave, saw-tooth) targeted at the back of the neck using personal fans in a warm ambient environment (27.5°C).

measures.instrument: Wireless iButtons (12 sites, Hardy and Du Bois weighting)

measures.construct: Rate of change in local skin temperature (dTsk,l)

findings.antecedent: Strong subjective discomfort
findings.mechanism: Alliesthesia operates even without strong discomfort, challenging the traditional view.
findings.quote: strong subjective discomfort is not a necessary precondition for thermal pleasure.

findings.antecedent: Physiological thermoneutral zone
findings.mechanism: Alliesthesia is less pronounced and more ambiguous in moderate scenarios within the thermoneutral zone.
findings.quote: Alliesthesia remained viable even within the physiological thermoneutral zone, although it was less pronounced and more ambiguous

findings.antecedent: Moderate local skin temperature changes (contrapuntal to whole-body mean skin temperature) during innocuous exposures at margins of thermal comfort zone
findings.mechanism: The contrast between local and whole-body thermal states elicits pleasure.
findings.quote: Positive hedonic tones were elicited during innocuous exposures at the margins of the thermal comfort zone by applying moderate local skin temperature changes that were contrapuntal to the whole-body, mean skin temperature.

findings.antecedent: Local skin temperature changes (contrapuntal to whole-body thermal state) in warm and cool conditions
findings.mechanism: Locally applied stimuli contrasting the whole-body thermal state can elicit pleasure.
findings.quote: In both warm and cool conditions, whole-body thermal pleasure was elicited from locally applied stimuli that contrast the whole-body thermal state.

findings.antecedent: Thermal environmental stimuli (localized and whole-body)
findings.mechanism: Pronounced between-subject variability in hedonic responses to thermal stimuli.
findings.quote: the hedonic tone attached to thermal environmental stimuli, both localised and whole-body, exhibited pronounced between-subject variability.

findings.antecedent: Intensity of subjects’ displeasure in preconditioning environment
findings.consequent: Tone and magnitude of thermal pleasure response to localised thermal stimuli
findings.mechanism: Higher initial displeasure creates a greater 'load-error' that can be corrected by the stimulus, leading to more pleasure.
moderators_reported: intensity of displeasure in preconditioning environment
findings.quote: The most useful variable for distinguishing the tone and magnitude of thermal pleasure response to localised thermal stimuli was the intensity of the subjects’ displeasure in the preconditioning environment.

findings.antecedent: Magnitude of change in local skin temperature
findings.consequent: Perceived pleasantness of localised thermal stimuli
findings.mechanism: Larger changes in local skin temperature contribute more to perceived pleasantness.
findings.quote: The magnitude of change in local skin temperature also had a significant effect on perceived pleasantness of localised thermal stimuli.

findings.antecedent: Initial skin temperature and initial thermal pleasure status
findings.mechanism: These parameters are good predictors, improving correct prediction close to 90%.
findings.quote: Initial skin temperature and initial thermal pleasure status were shown to very good predictors of the hedonic response to localised warming, in some instances improving correct prediction close to 90%.

findings.antecedent: Corrective temperature step-change (Paper 2)
findings.mechanism: Thermal pleasure increased proportionally to the physiological load error incurred, indicating a corrective effect.
findings.quote: The intensity of thermal pleasure immediately following a corrective temperature step-change increased proportionally to the physiological load error incurred

findings.antecedent: Temperature step-change (Paper 2, Sequence A1)
findings.quote: No change in thermal pleasure (Tples) was registered by subjects during Sequence A1

findings.antecedent: Temperature step-change (Paper 2, Sequence B1)
findings.quote: only a small decrease in Sequence B1.

findings.antecedent: Local stimulation (fan in warm, heat lamps in cool) (Paper 2, Sequences A2 and B2)
findings.mechanism: Local stimulation can generate positive hedonic tone even when mild displeasure precedes it.
findings.quote: Mild displeasure (negative Tples) preceded the initiation of behavioural control actions for Sequence A2 and B2, but local stimulation generated a positive change in hedonic tone.

findings.antecedent: Radiant heating (heat lamps) during downward temperature ramping (Paper 2, Sequence B3)
findings.mechanism: Radiant heating was effective at minimizing heat loss, preventing deterioration in pleasure.
findings.quote: the effectiveness of the heat lamps in minimizing body heat loss... can be seen in the resistance of thermal pleasure votes to register any deterioration – in fact there was a small but insignificant increase in thermal pleasure.

findings.antecedent: Sequences A4 and B4 (Paper 2)
findings.quote: Clearly the largest positive increments in thermal pleasure votes were registered after Sequences A4 and B4.

findings.antecedent: Change in skin temperature (Paper 2)
findings.mechanism: Strong negative correlation for warm exposures (A1-A4) and strong positive correlation for cool exposures (B1-B4).
findings.quote: A Pearson correlation indicated a strong negative correlation between the change in skin temperature and the change in thermal pleasure (r = −0.66; p < 0.01) for the warm exposures (Sequences A1–A4), and a strong positive correlation (r = 0.65; p < 0.01) for the cool exposures (Sequences B1–B4).

findings.antecedent: Localized convective cooling (fan) at back of subject (Paper 2, Sequence A2)
findings.quote: Localized convective cooling applied to the back of the subject in Sequence A2 increased thermal pleasure for approximately seven minutes

findings.antecedent: Local skin temperature changing in opposing direction to mean condition (Paper 2)
findings.mechanism: Spatial alliesthesia is driven by contrasting local and mean skin temperature trends.
findings.quote: There was a positive change in thermal pleasure ratings as local skin temperature changed in the opposing direction to the mean condition.

findings.antecedent: Mean and local skin temperatures converging due to diminishing efficacy of convective cooling (Paper 2, Sequence A1)
findings.mechanism: Negative alliesthesia occurs when stimuli exacerbate thermoregulatory load-error.
findings.quote: Displeasure occurred in Sequence A1 as mean and local skin temperatures converged because of the diminishing efficacy of convective cooling in the upward ramping air temperature, with negative alliesthesia continuing as both skin temperatures warmed at a similar rate.

findings.antecedent: Heat lamps (Paper 2, Sequence B2)
findings.consequent: Divergent skin temperatures and sustained positive alliesthesia
findings.quote: the heat lamps in Sequence B2 maintained divergent skin temperatures and positive alliesthesia was sustained for ten minutes.

findings.antecedent: Transition away from neutral thermal environmental exposure (Paper 2, Sequence 1)
findings.quote: A decrease in mean thermal pleasure was observed when subjects transitioned away from a neutral thermal environmental exposure (Figure 7), regardless of whether the direction was towards warmer or cooler ambient temperatures (Sequence 1).

findings.antecedent: Corrective transitions within the thermoneutral zone (Paper 2)
findings.mechanism: Positive pleasure can be experienced even with negligible or non-existent core temperature changes.
findings.quote: subjects of this experiment reported positive pleasure following corrective transitions within the thermoneutral zone (Figure 7) where core temperature changes were negligible or non-existent (Figure 5).

findings.antecedent: Localized warming to hands and feet (Paper 3)
findings.mechanism: Local stimuli can influence global thermal sensation.
findings.quote: to test if whole-body thermal perceptions are influenced by warm stimuli applied to distal sites (hand or feet) in cool exposures

findings.antecedent: Applying local warming (Paper 3)
findings.quote: Applying local warming had a significant increase (p < 0.05) on global (whole-body) thermal sensation (Tsens,g) for both feet and hand warming.

findings.antecedent: Thermal stimulation of feet and hands (Paper 3)
findings.consequent: Distinction between global (Tsens,g) and local (Tsens,l) sensation
findings.quote: subjects could distinguish between their global sensation (Tsens,g) and their local sensation (Tsens,l) during periods of thermal stimulation of the feet and hands.

findings.antecedent: Local stimulation (Paper 3)
findings.quote: local stimulation produced a highly significant (p < 0.01) non-zero change in hedon units for both foot warming (t(27) = 4.973) and hand warming (t(46) = 7.899).

findings.antecedent: Local heating applied to foot (Paper 3)
findings.consequent: Positive change in thermal pleasure votes
findings.quote: When heating was applied locally to the foot, 59% of participants experienced a predominantly positive change in thermal pleasure votes

findings.antecedent: Local heating applied to hand (Paper 3)
findings.consequent: Positive change in thermal pleasure votes
findings.quote: Hand warming only had a predominantly positive effect on 37% of participants.

findings.antecedent: Pre-onset Tples, pre-onset Tsk,l, and ΔTsk,l after 3 min (Paper 3, onset period)
findings.mechanism: These variables significantly differentiate hedonic response clusters during the onset of warming.
findings.quote: pre-onset Tples, pre-onset Tsk,l and ΔTsk,l after 3 min were significantly different between clusters during the onset period of warming.

findings.antecedent: Pre-onset Tsk,l and ΔTsk,l after 5 min (Paper 3, tail period)
findings.mechanism: These variables significantly differentiate hedonic response clusters during the tail period of warming.
findings.quote: Both the pre-onset Tsk,l and the ΔTsk,l after 5 min were significantly different (p < 0.05) between collapsed clusters in the tail period.

findings.antecedent: Lower local skin temperatures and more local warming in first 3 min (Paper 3, onset period)
findings.quote: Participants with a positive hedonic trend during the onset period had lower local skin temperatures and received more local warming in the first 3 min than those with a negative voting trend.

findings.antecedent: Warmer pre-onset skin temperature and larger magnitude of local warming after 5 min (Paper 3, tail period)
findings.quote: Subjects with a negatively trending ΔTples during the tail period had a warmer pre-onset skin temperature and experienced a larger magnitude of local warming after 5 min than those with a positive trend.

findings.antecedent: Onset period variables (pre-onset Tples, pre-onset Tsk,l, ΔTsk,l) (Paper 3)
findings.quote: The onset model explained 60% (Nagelkerke R2) of the variance in hedonic response

findings.antecedent: Tail period variables (pre-onset Tsk,l, ΔTsk,l) (Paper 3)
findings.quote: whilst the tail model was less successful at 23% (Nagelkerke R2).

findings.antecedent: 1 unit increase in pre-onset Tples (Paper 3, onset period)
findings.quote: the likelihood of a participant in this experiment having a negative hedonic response from local warming in the onset period was 3.18 times greater per unit increase in pre-onset Tples.

findings.antecedent: 1 unit increase in pre-onset Tsk,l (Paper 3, onset period)
findings.quote: the change in odds from the observed difference in pre-onset Tsk,l accounted for the largest increase in the odds of a negative hedonic response from local warming during the onset period.

findings.antecedent: 1°C increase in ΔTsk,l after 3 min (Paper 3, onset period)
findings.quote: A 1°C increase in ΔTsk,l after 3 min reduced the likelihood of a negative response during the onset period.

findings.antecedent: 1 unit increase in pre-onset Tsk,l (Paper 3, tail period)
1 unit increase in ΔTsk,l (Paper 3, tail period)
findings.quote: participants receiving higher levels of local heating after 5 min being twice as likely to respond negatively.

findings.antecedent: Elevated air movement (Paper 4)
findings.quote: elevated air movement significantly increased average thermal pleasure (F(2.973,80.267) = 22.349, p < 0.0005)

findings.antecedent: Elevated air movement (Paper 4)
findings.quote: significantly decreased skin temperature (F(3.057,103.936) = 121.737, p < 0.0005)

findings.antecedent: Elevated air movement (Paper 4)
findings.quote: thermal sensation significantly decreased (F(4,136) = 14.768, p < 0.0005) when compared with pre-fan votes

findings.antecedent: Different air movement patterns (constant, sinusoidal, square-wave, saw-tooth) (Paper 4)
findings.quote: there were no significant perceptual or physiological differences (p < 0.05) between the air movement patterns.

findings.antecedent: First air movement profile in sequence (Paper 4)
findings.quote: subjects reported feeling significantly cooler during the first air movement profile only when compared with the fourth air movement profile (p < 0.005) irrespective of the pattern type

findings.antecedent: First sequence of air movement (Paper 4)
findings.consequent: Peak rate of change in skin temperature (dTsk)
findings.quote: the peak rate of change in skin temperature (dTsk) was also significantly greater in the first sequence (p < 0.005).

findings.antecedent: Subjects' pre-fan psychometric votes of thermal sensation (Paper 4)
findings.consequent: Change in thermal sensation votes from elevated air movement
findings.quote: subjects’ pre-fan psychometric votes of thermal sensation (r = −0.894, n = 28, p = 0.000) [...] were highly correlated with the change in respective votes resulting from elevated air movement

findings.antecedent: Subjects' pre-fan psychometric votes of thermal pleasure (Paper 4)
findings.consequent: Change in thermal pleasure votes from elevated air movement
findings.quote: thermal pleasure (r = −0.552, n = 28, p = 0.002) were highly correlated with the change in respective votes resulting from elevated air movement

findings.antecedent: Feeling warm during pre-fan period (Paper 4)
findings.consequent: Larger change in thermal sensation vote after fans switched on
findings.quote: Subjects who reported feeling warm during the period without fans had a larger change in thermal sensation vote after fans were switched on.

findings.antecedent: Experiencing mild displeasure in pre-fan conditions (Paper 4)
findings.consequent: Greater positive shift in thermal pleasure under elevated air movement
findings.quote: subjects experiencing mild displeasure in the pre-fan conditions had a greater positive shift in thermal pleasure under elevated air movement than those who were indifferent to the warm, still conditions.

findings.antecedent: Pre-fan thermal pleasure votes (Paper 4)
findings.consequent: Magnitude of pleasure response to elevated air movement
findings.quote: The most significant difference between clusters was the pre-fan thermal pleasure votes (p < 0.01).

findings.antecedent: Stronger initial heat-discomfort (Paper 4)
findings.quote: the stronger the initial heat-discomfort, the greater the thermal pleasure resulting from the fans.

findings.antecedent: Convective heat loss on the neck (Paper 4)
findings.quote: the convective heat loss on the neck was significantly greater (p < 0.05) for the subjects with a modest change in thermal pleasure.

findings.antecedent: First sequence of elevated air movement (Paper 4)
findings.quote: The group of the subjects who had a large increase in thermal pleasure had a sustained pleasure response for the entire period of elevated air movement. However, those with only a moderate increase saw a positive shift for the first sequence before pleasure votes slowly decayed back towards pre-fan levels.

findings.antecedent: Skin temperature on the back of the neck (Paper 4)
findings.quote: Skin temperature on the back of the neck exhibited the same trend for both clusters, but the magnitude of cooling was greater for those with a moderate increase in thermal pleasure.

mechanisms: Dynamic discharge rate of cutaneous thermoreceptors
Local skin temperature changes contrapuntal to whole-body mean skin temperature
Physiological load-error (deviation from preferred thermal state)
Heightened sensitivity of the cold thermosensory system
Rate of change in skin temperature
Anticipatory responses within the spatial alliesthesial framework of behavioural thermoregulation
Feed-forward thermal perception loop based on skin thermoreceptor signals
moderators: Intensity of displeasure in the preconditioning environment
Magnitude of change in local skin temperature
implementation_implications: Leverage alliesthesia through peripheral thermal stimulation in regular indoor environments.
Increase occupant satisfaction and reduce energy consumption through targeted thermal stimulation delivered locally by Personal Environmental Control (PEC) systems.
PEC systems can create bespoke personal-microclimates tuned to individual cutaneous thermal sensibilities.
Dissatisfaction can transform into thermal pleasure if corrective localized stimuli are provided.
Widening central set-point temperatures can lead to energy savings.
Deliberate introduction of temperature drifts, air movement, and thermal asymmetries in building design.

limitations: Lack of randomization in the sequence of exposures to control for order effects (Paper 2, 3, 4).
Low statistical power for testing gender differences due to small sample sizes (Paper 2, 3, 4).
Potential for subject fatigue during long experiments (Paper 2).
Potential for subjects to influence each other during voting (Paper 2).
Actual position of subjects in conceptual physiological zones was not measured (Paper 2).
Differences in duration and total area of contact warming between the hand and feet may have complicated findings (Paper 3).

Modest levels of heat loss and skin temperature dynamics from brief periods of elevated air movement may have resulted in subtle effects, explaining no significant perceptual differences between air movement patterns (Paper 4).
